reason: The EU requirement first appears in 2025 (AI Act alignment and enforcement structures) and the only later EU item, in 2026, concerns the AI Factory Antenna, so there is no repeated EU wording to compare; the chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. Separately, national sources show the gap is older than the EU ask: a 2024 government plan mentions AI as a future need, and the 2025 audit traces a stalled strategy to a 2021 working group, but these are one-year snapshots rather than a trend. The value therefore means new as an EU requirement, not new as a national gap.

Against the single EU alignment ask of 2025, the responding AI legislation and AI strategy are still proposed, and the adopted ICT strategy and signed Antenna grant do not supply alignment or enforcement; these statuses are themselves proposals. What remains is alignment with the AI Act and the enforcement structures it needs, none of which yet exists. National sources confirm the absence (machine-translated audit, capped at Medium), and the audit's statement that data protection law is aligned with the GDPR conflicts with the Commission's statement that full alignment is pending, which is left unresolved.

The rating rests only on the EU layer: one body-text invitation in the 2025 report to align fully with the AI Act, plus a 2026 readout that encourages outreach and does not mention the Act. It is not a benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition, is absent from the 2025 Chapter 10 key recommendations and is not repeated, so it cannot be High; Medium reflects a requirement central to the AI theme with thin support. The much larger national audit, strategy and research evidence (over 200 of 229 items, mostly from a few documents) describes the gap but was given no weight here.

Drafting is within government control, with the EU Act as a template and AI legislation already listed in an adopted action plan, but enforcement structures need a designated authority, specialist staff and funding, across several bodies. The record is weak: one working group meeting since 2021, a digital assistant no longer functioning and no line of accountability between the ministry and the innovation fund, though a data protection law gives some base and an EU-funded Antenna grant is signed. This leans on machine-translated national evidence (capped at Medium), and the audit's finding that no public sector project has been implemented sits against its report of the Buki platform at a state university, a difference of scope it does not explain.

The key recommendation to finalise and adopt the ICT strategy ran unchanged from 2020 to 2024 and gave way in 2025 to a report that the strategy and action plan were adopted, so the default to persistent no longer holds for that strand; the chapter scale (some progress 2020, limited 2021 to 2024, some 2025) is context only and was not decisive. The capacity wording is unchanged across 2022 to 2025, so this movement is partial and in requirements rather than results, and adoption is not success.

The latest EU items report the strategy adopted but still ask for stronger ministry capacity, more IT staff and the digital agency, which remains proposed and which the country has said it will reassess; these statuses are themselves proposals, and that of the National Council is unclear because the 2024 audit found no 2023 activity while the strategy cites its formation. What remains is applying the strategy, building coordinating capacity and IT staffing, and settling the agency question. The Commission's well-structured set-up and the national vacuum are a noted difference of scope, not a conflict.

The ICT strategy was a Chapter 10 key recommendation in five successive reports, and the ministry capacity ask has recurred in four reports to 2025, on an issue central to the digital transformation theme. The key recommendation itself left the list after adoption in 2025 and the capacity ask sits in body text, so High rests on treating adoption as the start rather than the end of the requirement. National plans and audits were not counted towards this rating.

A new ministry and an adopted strategy show that institutional steps can be taken, but the strategy took over five years and coordination depends on many institutions that have offered limited cooperation. IT posts are about half filled and public pay rules limit competition with the private sector, which the ministry cannot change alone. The staffing and working group evidence is machine translated and capped at Medium.

The Commission's 2023 call for basic systems became Reform Agenda steps in 2024, and in 2025 the electronic archiving law was adopted and technical checks found the document system partially operational; the chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. Use has barely moved, however, from 21 institutions in 2022 to 22 in 2025, on machine-translated national figures capped at Medium, so the improvement is mainly legal. The 0.01% inclusion figure in the 2023 strategy does not fit its own count of 20 institutions and was not relied on.

Of the three Reform Agenda requirements, the law is adopted and the Commission treats that step as achieved, but it applied only from June 2026 with by-laws still proposed, the e-platform is proposed and the document system is only partially operational; these statuses are themselves proposals. What remains is application of the law, the storage and record-keeping platform, the single document system across all central institutions and the digital mailbox. No item in the input shows whether the 2026 deadlines were met.

The archiving law, the storage platform and the single document system are named Reform Agenda steps with payments attached, and these shared systems are central to the digital government theme. The rating rests on those EU conditions, not on the many national plan items.

The tasks are bounded, led by one ministry and backed by payment incentives, and the legal step was achieved by its 2025 deadline. Roll-out is harder: it needs hardware, licences, training and change of working habits in many institutions, and earlier piloting left 22 institutions using a small part of the system. The national evidence on use is machine translated and capped at Medium.

The Commission's wording is close to unchanged across reports: advancing but low in 2020 to 2023, advancing slowly in 2024 and 2025, and low in 2026, with one 2025 note that SME adoption has accelerated but stays uneven and basic. The chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. The 54.5% website figure repeats across reports and was not treated as new evidence, and the 3% and 19.7% online sales figures use different populations, so they show no trend.

The latest EU asks concern support to companies through the innovation hub and active use of Digital Europe calls; the hub is set up and the association agreement signed, while vouchers, the support portal and the grant mechanism are proposed, and these statuses are themselves proposals. What remains is actual use of these channels and SME adoption beyond basic technologies, as the Commission still reported low digitalisation in 2026.

The finding is repeated in most years, largely in economic governance documents, but it has few specific recommendations; the only key recommendation found is the 2025 hub item, and no benchmark or payment condition names it in the input. It is therefore a repeated EU concern that is not central to accession steps.

Government can fund and steer support, and EU programmes and a first hub already exist, but results depend on many small firms' demand, skills and finance. Past effort is small and not evaluated: EUR 0.5 million budgeted in 2023, and the strategy itself says there has been no support mechanism for projects of greater national importance; that source is machine translated and capped at Medium.

The ask to align with the Digital Services Act and Digital Markets Act recurs with little change in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports, and e-commerce was described as slow in 2021, 2022 and 2023. The chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. Growth figures for online transactions are country-reported, partly repeated and on differing bases, so they were not read as closing the issue.

The latest EU items still require alignment with the DSA, DMA and Geo-blocking Regulation, and the responding alignment measures are all proposed, with national targets of 2027 and 2028 and only training delivered; these statuses are themselves proposals. What remains is the alignment itself for all these acts, plus full alignment on electronic commerce. The country's report of being largely aligned with the e-Commerce Directive and the Commission's call to align fully differ in degree and speaker, and were not treated as closure.

The requirement is repeated in three reports and relates to binding acquis, but it sits in Chapter 10 body text, not in the 2024 or 2025 key recommendations, and is not named as a benchmark or payment condition in the input. It is therefore a repeated EU requirement that is not central under the criteria.

The work is mainly legislative with EU texts as templates, a government timetable and a request for expert group participation, which depends partly on the Commission. No draft is reported and past progress is limited to training, and applying platform rules will need capacity that the input does not evidence.

The alignment ask on digital tools in company law recurs in near-identical wording in 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, so the default applies; the chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. The 2025 screening finding of a high level of alignment shows the remaining ask is narrow, but it is not evidence of change over time.

Fully online company registration is in practice and the Commission finds high alignment, on a status that is itself a proposal. What remains is further alignment with Directive (EU) 2019/1151, including scrutiny of a company's object and verification of directors' appointment and disqualification. The country's statement that it is aligned and the Commission's statement that further alignment is necessary are a confirmed contradiction, reported here and not resolved.

It appears in the key recommendations of three reports, but always bundled with other company law items, and digital tools are a narrow strand on which the Commission already finds high alignment. It is therefore a repeated EU requirement that is not central to the chapter, and it is not a benchmark or payment condition in the input.

The remaining points are specific legal amendments in a field with few actors and a working one-stop-shop registry, and they depend on no other institution's roll-out. The ask has nonetheless stood since 2021 with no reported draft, which is why the rating depends on the small scope and not on past momentum.
